items.ask: Give the principal stretches of finite simple shear with amount of shear γ.
items.answer: λ = √(1 + γ²/4) ± γ/2. Their product is 1 (isochoric) and their difference is γ. For γ = 1.5 they are 2 and 0.5.
items.cue: Product one, difference γ: λ₁λ₂ = 1 and λ₁ − λ₂ = γ pin both roots.

items.ask: What do the eigenvectors of U and of V represent in F = RU = VR?
items.answer: Eigenvectors N of U are the material principal directions in the reference body; eigenvectors n of V are the same fibres in the current body, with n = RN. U and V share the principal stretches.
items.cue: U looks back at the reference, V looks at the current shape; R swings each N onto its n.

items.ask: Give the current angle θ between fibres that started along e₁ and e₂, in terms of C.
items.answer: cos θ = C₁₂/√(C₁₁C₂₂). The finite shear angle is the drop from 90°, γ₁₂ = 90° − θ, so sin γ₁₂ = C₁₂/√(C₁₁C₂₂).
items.cue: C is the metric: a dot product divided by the product of the two lengths, as for any pair of vectors.

items.ask: Define the infinitesimal rotation tensor and state when it represents R.
items.answer: ω = ½(H − Hᵀ), the skew part of the displacement gradient H. It approximates R − I when strains and rotations are both small.
items.cue: Split H into a symmetric half (strain) and a skew half (spin); skew means rotation.

items.ask: Why does a twisted stick of chalk or a glass rod crack along a 45° helix?
items.answer: The surface is in pure shear τ, whose principal stresses ±τ act at 45° to the axis. Brittle materials fail in tension, so the crack opens normal to σ₁ = τ and spirals at 45°.
items.cue: Draw Mohr's circle of pure shear: centred at the origin, σ₁ = τ sits 90° round the circle, 45° on the part.

items.ask: Give the octahedral shear stress in principal stresses and its link to von Mises stress.
items.answer: τ_oct = (1/3)√((σ₁ − σ₂)² + (σ₂ − σ₃)² + (σ₃ − σ₁)²) = (√2/3)σ_vm.
items.cue: The octahedral plane leans equally on all three axes: one third of the root sum of squared differences.

items.ask: State the stress state at a point on a traction-free surface with unit normal n.
items.answer: σn = 0, so σ_nn, σ_nt and σ_ns all vanish. The normal n is a principal direction with principal stress 0, and the remaining stresses lie in the tangent plane (plane stress).
items.cue: Free surface: n is a principal axis carrying zero; everything else lives in the surface plane.

items.ask: List the five independent constants of a transversely isotropic solid with fibre axis 1, and the dependent sixth.
items.answer: E₁, E₂, ν₁₂, ν₂₃ and G₁₂. The isotropic 2-3 plane supplies G₂₃ = E₂/(2(1 + ν₂₃)), and symmetry gives ν₂₁/E₂ = ν₁₂/E₁.
items.cue: Two moduli, two Poisson ratios, one axial shear; the isotropic plane makes its own shear like any isotropic sheet.

items.ask: Write isotropic Hooke's law in Lamé form and give λ and μ in terms of E and ν.
items.answer: σ = λ tr(ε) I + 2με, with μ = E/(2(1 + ν)) and λ = Eν/((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)).
items.cue: λ handles volume, 2μ handles shape; λ blows up at ν = ½ just like K.

items.ask: Give the kink band compressive strength of a unidirectional ply and its value for perfect alignment.
items.answer: σ_c = τ_y/(γ_y + φ), with τ_y the matrix shear yield stress, γ_y = τ_y/G₁₂ and φ the initial fibre misalignment. At φ = 0 it equals G₁₂ (Rosen shear mode); φ = γ_y (about 1° for carbon/epoxy) halves it.
items.cue: Misalignment sits in the denominator: the more the fibres lean, the sooner the matrix gives way in shear.

items.ask: Write the stresses from an Airy stress function in polar coordinates.
items.cue: Hoop is the plain second radial derivative; the shear keeps the Cartesian minus sign.

items.ask: Give the hoop stress on the edge of a circular hole under remote principal stresses σ₁ and σ₂.
items.answer: σ_θθ(a, θ) = (σ₁ + σ₂) − 2(σ₁ − σ₂)cos 2θ, with θ measured from σ₁. Peak 3σ₁ − σ₂ at θ = 90°; minimum 3σ₂ − σ₁ at θ = 0.
items.cue: Uniaxial gives 3 and −1; superpose two of them at right angles.

items.ask: How does the hoop stress decay from a hole along the line transverse to uniaxial tension σ?
items.answer: σ_θθ = σ(1 + a²/(2r²) + 3a⁴/(2r⁴)): 3σ at the edge, about 1.22σ at r = 2a and 1.07σ at r = 3a.
items.cue: Inverse square plus inverse fourth power: the disturbance dies within a few radii, Saint-Venant style.

items.ask: Give the Lamé radial and hoop stresses in a thick cylinder under internal pressure p alone.
items.answer: σ_rr = (pa²/(b² − a²))(1 − b²/r²) and σ_θθ = (pa²/(b² − a²))(1 + b²/r²). Hoop stress is greatest at the bore.
items.cue: A ± B/r²: minus for radial, plus for hoop; check σ_rr = −p at r = a and 0 at r = b.

items.ask: What is autofrettage and why does it help a gun barrel or high-pressure vessel?
items.answer: A one-time overpressure that yields the bore. On unloading, the elastic outer layers squeeze the bore into residual hoop compression, which lowers the peak working hoop stress and extends fatigue life.
items.cue: Pre-stretch the inside so the outside clamps it: built-in compression waiting to cancel service tension.

items.ask: For a thick cylinder under internal pressure p, how does the bore hoop stress change as b/a grows?
items.answer: σ_θθ(a) = p(b² + a²)/(b² − a²) falls toward p. Beyond about b = 2a to 3a extra wall buys little, and p is the floor.
items.cue: (k² + 1)/(k² − 1) tends to 1: even an infinite wall sees hoop stress p at the bore.

items.ask: Give the inflation pressure of a thin incompressible Mooney-Rivlin spherical balloon.
items.answer: P = (4H/R)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷)(C₁ + C₂λ²), from P = (H/(Rλ²))dW/dλ. With C₂ > 0 the pressure climbs again at large stretch.
items.cue: Neo-Hookean factor times (C₁ + C₂λ²); set C₂ = 0 and μ = 2C₁ to recover 2μ(H/R)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷).

items.ask: State the universal relation for simple shear of an isotropic elastic solid.
items.answer: σ₁₁ − σ₂₂ = γσ₁₂, valid for every isotropic hyperelastic material at any amount of shear γ.
items.cue: B₁₁ − B₂₂ = γ² = γB₁₂, so the material constants cancel.

items.ask: What does the C₂ term of W = C₁(I₁ − 3) + C₂(I₂ − 3) add, and what is the small-strain shear modulus?
items.answer: The C₂ term depends on I₂, the area-stretch invariant, and stiffens equibiaxial and large stretches. The small-strain shear modulus is μ = 2(C₁ + C₂).
items.cue: I₁ tracks squared lengths, I₂ tracks squared areas; each C contributes twice itself to μ.

items.ask: State the local balance of linear momentum in the current and the reference configuration.
items.answer: Current: div σ + ρb = ρ Dv/Dt. Reference: Div P + ρ₀b = ρ₀ ∂²x/∂t², with P the first Piola stress.
items.cue: Same law, two bookkeepers: Cauchy pairs with ρ and x, Piola pairs with ρ₀ and X.

items.ask: State conservation of mass in Lagrangian and Eulerian forms.
items.answer: Lagrangian: ρJ = ρ₀. Eulerian: Dρ/Dt + ρ div v = 0, equivalently ∂ρ/∂t + div(ρv) = 0.
items.cue: A parcel keeps its mass: shrink its volume by J and its density rises by the same factor.

items.ask: Give the material rate of the volume ratio J.
items.answer: DJ/Dt = J div v = J tr D.
items.cue: Volume grows at the rate the velocity field spreads out: the divergence.

items.ask: In a thick cylinder with a hot bore in steady conduction, what is the sign of the hoop stress at each surface?
items.answer: Hoop compression at the hot bore and hoop tension at the cooler outer surface. T varies with ln r, σ_rr = 0 at both faces, and the hoop force across the wall sums to zero. A cold bore flips every sign.
items.cue: The hot part wants to grow and gets squeezed; the cool part gets stretched to hold it.

items.ask: Give the thermal surface stress in a thin wall with a linear through-thickness difference ΔT and restrained bending.
items.answer: σ = ±EαΔT/(2(1 − ν)), equal biaxial: compressive on the hot face and tensile on the cool face.
items.cue: Half of the fully restrained plate value EαΔT/(1 − ν), since each face is ΔT/2 from the mean.

items.ask: Give the longitudinal thermal expansion coefficient of a unidirectional ply.
items.answer: α₁ = (E_fα_fV_f + E_mα_mV_m)/(E_fV_f + E_mV_m): a stiffness-weighted average, close to the fibre value because the stiff fibres dominate.
items.cue: Tug of war between phases: weight each α by its E times its volume fraction.
